sentences.text: Trilophosuchus is an extinct genus of mekosuchine crocodilian that lived in Australia.
The name Trilophosuchus translates to "triple-crested crocodile" and refers to three parallel ridges running along the skull table.
The snout of Trilophosuchus is thought to have been very robust with a trapezoid cross-section just before the eyes.
Trilophosuchus possesses a unique acute dural peak above the hindbrain, a feature shared only with Agaresuchus and Arenysuchus among eusuchians.
The skull of Trilophosuchus measures only 79 mm from the back of the head to the front of the rostrum, indicating a very small size.
The holotype skull was uncovered in 1985 and is considered one of the best-preserved fossil crocodilians from Australia despite missing the snout.
The genus Trilophosuchus was erected in 1993 by Paul Willis of the University of New South Wales, who published the name in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.
The species name rackhami honors Alan Rackham Senior, a supporter of the Riversleigh excavations.
Researchers propose that Trilophosuchus was restricted to small prey, analogous to small agamas and iguanas, fitting its small body size compared to larger terrestrial crocodylomorphs.
Evidence of skull bone fusion and surface sculpting indicates that the holotype specimen of Trilophosuchus was an adult when it died.
Researchers suggest that Trilophosuchus was a dwarf species exhibiting juvenile-like traits due to paedomorphy rather than being an immature individual.
Trilophosuchus belongs to the subfamily Mekosuchinae, a group of endemic Australian and New Caledonian crocodiles.
Despite resembling early crocodyliforms, Trilophosuchus is classified as an advanced crocodilian.
Only a single species, T. rackhami, has been described for the genus Trilophosuchus.

Trilophosuchus lived in the early Miocene, approximately 20 million years ago, though other estimates suggest a broader range from the Chattian to the Serravallian, between 27.3 and 11.63 million years ago.
Fossils of Trilophosuchus have been found at the Ringtail Site in north-western Queensland, dating to the Miocene epoch.
Additional remains found at the older Hiatus Site extend the known range of Trilophosuchus into the Oligocene.

The Ringtail Site where Trilophosuchus fossils were found preserves evidence of a pool in a forested karst terrain that included aquatic animals like lungfish, turtles, and the extinct platypus Obdurodon dicksoni.
It is debated whether the Oligocene material found at the Hiatus Site represents a second species of Trilophosuchus or simply age-related variation.
A 2018 study by Stein et al. placed Trilophosuchus as a basal form related to Ultrastenos, a result later deemed irregular due to problematic taxa.
It is unclear how Trilophosuchus and Mekosuchus sanderi differed in their ecology despite both being thought to be terrestrial animals.
